objective: Determine what should be written in a teaching poster prompt
prompt:
This chapter uses Qwen-Image-2.1-Turbo to generate a chemistry knowledge poster. Which of the following should be written into the prompt? (Multiple choice)

A. Knowledge points and reaction equations that have already been verified, given as in the original text
B. Image regions and reading order, e.g., experimental apparatus on the left, phenomena and conclusions on the right
C. Let the model complete chemical equations it is unsure about on its own, so the image will be more complete
D. Output parameters such as size and quantity, as well as pseudo-text/typos to avoid
E. After generation, proofread the text on the poster word by word, then decide whether to use it
reference: C is the opposite of the intent: equations on the poster must come from verified knowledge content; letting the model complete them on its own would lock errors into teaching materials. The approach in this chapter is to organize "already verified knowledge content" into the prompt, rather than letting the model guess.
explanation:
The focus of this chapter is not "AI can draw images," but "how to make the drawn images usable for teaching."

A: Knowledge content must be verified first. The approach in this chapter is to organize experimental phenomena, reaction equations, and key knowledge points into part of the prompt; the model is responsible for presentation, not invention.

B: Teaching posters have a reading order. Clearly specifying regions (before/after experiment, apparatus/phenomena/conclusions) is more effective than piling up adjectives; otherwise the model will place elements randomly, looking lively but failing to explain clearly.

D: Parameters such as size, quantity, and random seed determine reproducibility; negative constraints (no pseudo-text, no typos, no extra apparatus) can significantly reduce rework.

E: Text generated by image models can still be wrong, especially chemical formula subscripts and Chinese terminology. After generation, it must be proofread word by word; this is also why this chapter repeatedly emphasizes "check and adjust based on the results."

C is wrong because it treats the generative model as a knowledge source. The cost of errors in teaching materials is high; even if an equation completed by the model looks reasonable, it cannot be adopted directly.

Grading boundary: the selected letters must exactly match the reference answer.

prompt: Choose a knowledge point you want to teach (physics, chemistry, biology, or history are all fine) and write a poster prompt that can be used directly with an image generation model: include which verified knowledge content to use, how the image is divided into regions, how the text is laid out, what must be avoided, and what checklist you will use to verify each item after generation.

llm_rubric.criteria: Whether knowledge content is separated from visual description; whether clear region division and reading order are given; whether size/text/negative constraints are included; whether a post-generation checklist is given (formulas, units, subscripts, terminology, text-image consistency)

reference:
Knowledge content: first list the facts that should appear on the poster, each of which can be traced to a textbook or verified material. For example, "Iron reacts with copper sulfate; the solution changes from blue to pale green, and a red solid deposits on the surface of the iron nail" and "Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu." Write the equation and the phenomena separately to avoid the model merging them into one sentence.

Layout: on the left, draw the comparison apparatus before and after the experiment; on the upper right, place the equation; on the lower right, place the phenomena and conclusion; the reading order is left to right and top to bottom. Use one sentence to state what goes in each region, without piling up adjectives.

Text: three levels—title, equation, keywords—with font sizes decreasing in that order; explicitly require Chinese and avoid English placeholders or pseudo-text.

Negative constraints: no extra instruments, no incorrect subscripts, no unverifiable data generated on the image, no watermark.

Parameters: choose the size according to the use (16:9 for courseware or 3:4 for posters), generate multiple images at once and pick one, and fix the random seed for reproducibility.

Checklist: whether the equation is balanced and subscripts are correct, whether colors and phenomena match the textbook, units and symbols, terminology wording, whether text and image correspond, and whether there is any extra information fabricated by the model. If any item fails, adjust the prompt and regenerate rather than manually editing the image to hide the problem.
explanation:
This question turns "let AI draw an image" into "let AI lay out verified knowledge."

The most critical distinction is between **knowledge content** and **visual description**. Knowledge content must come from verified materials; the model is only responsible for presentation. Visual description (regions, color scheme, composition) is the part where the model can freely exercise creativity. If the two are written together, the model easily treats "looks reasonable" as "factually correct."

Region division is not an aesthetic issue; it is a teaching issue. Readers need to know what to look at first and what to look at next; without regions, the model will place all elements evenly, resulting in high information density but unclear causality.

Negative constraints are often more effective than positive descriptions. Image models tend to "complete"; if you do not tell them what not to include, they will add instruments, arrows, and decorative text.

The checklist is the final gate. Chemical formula subscripts, unit capitalization, and terminology wording are all places where models easily make mistakes and humans can spot them at a glance; item-by-item verification is much more actionable than an overall "something feels wrong."

This question has no single answer; grading depends on whether it covers the five parts: knowledge, layout, text, negative constraints, and verification.
